claim: Leptomeningeal metastasis is associated with dismal prognosis and has few treatment options.
source: Leptomeningeal metastasis is associated with dismal prognosis and has few treatment options.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that reflects established clinical knowledge about leptomeningeal metastasis outcomes.

claim: Very little is known about the immune response to leptomeningeal metastasis.
source: However, very little is known about the immune response to leptomeningeal metastasis.
evidence: This statement acknowledges a gap in current scientific understanding.

claim: Tumor-specific CD8+ T cells were generated in deep cervical lymph nodes (dCLNs) in a mouse model of breast cancer leptomeningeal metastasis.
source: Here, by establishing an immunocompetent mouse model of breast cancer leptomeningeal metastasis, we found that tumor-specific CD8+ T cells were generated in deep cervical lymph nodes (dCLNs) and played an important role in controlling leptomeningeal metastasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the mouse model described in the manuscript.

claim: Tumor-specific CD8+ T cells played an important role in controlling leptomeningeal metastasis.
source: Here, by establishing an immunocompetent mouse model of breast cancer leptomeningeal metastasis, we found that tumor-specific CD8+ T cells were generated in deep cervical lymph nodes (dCLNs) and played an important role in controlling leptomeningeal metastasis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing CD8+ T cell depletion increased tumor growth and adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: T cells in dCLNs displayed a senescence phenotype in mice bearing cancer cells that preferentially colonized in leptomeningeal space.
source: Mechanistically, T cells in dCLNs displayed a senescence phenotype and their recruitment was impaired in mice bearing cancer cells that preferentially colonized in leptomeningeal space.
evidence: This is supported by data showing increased p53, p21, and SA-β-gal expression in dCLN T cells from LM mice.

claim: Recruitment of T cells was impaired in mice bearing cancer cells that preferentially colonized in leptomeningeal space.
source: Mechanistically, T cells in dCLNs displayed a senescence phenotype and their recruitment was impaired in mice bearing cancer cells that preferentially colonized in leptomeningeal space.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data showing reduced migration of LM-CD8+ T cells to meninges.

claim: Upregulation of p53 suppressed the transcription of VLA-4 in senescent dCLN T cells.
source: Upregulation of p53 suppressed the transcription of VLA-4 in senescent dCLN T cells and consequently inhibited their migration to the leptomeningeal compartment.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assays, ChIP-qPCR data, and experiments in Trp53-/- mice.

claim: p53-mediated suppression of VLA-4 inhibited T cell migration to the leptomeningeal compartment.
source: Upregulation of p53 suppressed the transcription of VLA-4 in senescent dCLN T cells and consequently inhibited their migration to the leptomeningeal compartment.
evidence: This is supported by migration assays and two-photon imaging showing impaired T cell trafficking.

claim: CD8+ T cells from the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with leptomeningeal metastasis exhibited senescence.
source: Clinically, CD8+ T cells from the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with leptomeningeal metastasis exhibited senescence and VLA-4 downregulation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased SA-β-gal+ CD8+ T cells in CSF from metastatic patients.

claim: CD8+ T cells from the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with leptomeningeal metastasis exhibited VLA-4 downregulation.
source: Clinically, CD8+ T cells from the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with leptomeningeal metastasis exhibited senescence and VLA-4 downregulation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data showing lower VLA-4 expression in CD8+ T cells from LM patients.

claim: CD8+ T cell immunosenescence drives leptomeningeal metastasis.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrated that CD8+ T cell immunosenescence drives leptomeningeal metastasis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing senescence impairs T cell function and promotes LM.

claim: Brain metastasis is associated with one of the worst clinical outcomes and has few therapeutic options.
source: Brain metastasis is associated with one of the worst clinical outcomes and has few therapeutic options (Ahluwalia et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The brain contains two distinctive compartments – parenchyma mainly consisting of cells and leptomeninges filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
source: The brain contains two distinctive compartments – parenchyma mainly consisting of cells and leptomeninges filled with cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (Valiente et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Very little is known about the unique microenvironment of leptomeningeal metastasis.
source: Despite tremendous progress has been made in understanding the interaction between tumor cells and resident cells in parenchymal metastasis, very little is known about the unique microenvironment of leptomeningeal metastasis (LM) (Boire et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement identifies a knowledge gap and is supported by a citation.

claim: LM is caused by cancer cells invading the leptomeninges, or CSF-filled spaces.
source: LM, which is caused by cancer cells invading the leptomeninges, or CSF-filled spaces, represents the worst outcome of cancer patients (Franzoi and Hortobagyi, 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: LM represents the worst outcome of cancer patients.
source: LM, which is caused by cancer cells invading the leptomeninges, or CSF-filled spaces, represents the worst outcome of cancer patients (Franzoi and Hortobagyi, 2019; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This clinical statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The incidence of breast cancer with LM ranges between 3% and 16%.
source: Despite the development of diagnostic techniques and advances in cancer treatment, the incidence of breast cancer with LM increases, ranges between 3% and 16% (Kushner and Cheung, 1992).
evidence: This epidemiological data is supported by a citation.

claim: The median survival from detection of LM is as low as 18 weeks.
source: Its median survival from detection is as low as 18 weeks, and 1-year survival is about 15% (Niwińska et al., 2013).
evidence: This clinical outcome data is supported by a citation.

claim: 1-year survival of LM is about 15%.
source: Its median survival from detection is as low as 18 weeks, and 1-year survival is about 15% (Niwińska et al., 2013).
evidence: This clinical outcome data is supported by a citation.

claim: Access of circulating immune cells to the brain is limited by the blood–brain barrier (BBB).
source: Access of circulating immune cells to the brain is limited by the blood–brain barrier (BBB).
evidence: This is established knowledge about BBB function.

claim: The brain has previously been considered as an immune-privileged organ.
source: Therefore, the brain has previously been considered as an immune-privileged organ.
evidence: This reflects historical scientific understanding.

claim: Functional lymphatic vessels have been identified in meninges.
source: Recently, the paradigm has shifted, as functional lymphatic vessels have been identified in meninges.
evidence: This is a recent discovery that shifted understanding of brain immunity.

claim: Immune cells and antigens in central nervous system (CNS) can be drained to deep cervical lymph nodes (dCLNs) via meningeal lymphatic system.
source: Immune cells and antigens in central nervous system (CNS) can be drained to deep cervical lymph nodes (dCLNs) via meningeal lymphatic system (Louveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Ablation of lymphatic vessels reduces the interaction between brain-specific T cells and dendritic cells (DC) in experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) mice.
source: Ablation of lymphatic vessels reduces the interaction between brain-specific T cells and dendritic cells (DC), and alleviates disease progression in experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) mice (Louveau et al., 2018), indicating that lymphatic drainage contributes to T cell activation in CNS.
evidence: This experimental finding is supported by a citation.

claim: Ablation of lymphatic vessels alleviates disease progression in experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) mice.
source: Ablation of lymphatic vessels reduces the interaction between brain-specific T cells and dendritic cells (DC), and alleviates disease progression in experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) mice (Louveau et al., 2018), indicating that lymphatic drainage contributes to T cell activation in CNS.
evidence: This experimental finding is supported by a citation.

claim: Lymphatic drainage contributes to T cell activation in CNS.
source: Ablation of lymphatic vessels reduces the interaction between brain-specific T cells and dendritic cells (DC), and alleviates disease progression in experimental allergic encephalomyelitis (EAE) mice (Louveau et al., 2018), indicating that lymphatic drainage contributes to T cell activation in CNS.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the cited experimental data.

claim: VLA-4 is a member of integrin family.
source: The very late activated Ag-4 (VLA-4) is a member of integrin family, which is widely known to mediate T cell adhesion to endothelium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VLA-4 molecular classification.

claim: VLA-4 is widely known to mediate T cell adhesion to endothelium.
source: The very late activated Ag-4 (VLA-4) is a member of integrin family, which is widely known to mediate T cell adhesion to endothelium.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VLA-4 function.

claim: VLA-4 functions as an essential adhesion molecule in T cell migration across the BBB in EAE.
source: In fact, VLA-4 functions as an essential adhesion molecule in T cell migration across the BBB in EAE (Bartholomäus et al., 2009; Schläger et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: The incidences of most cancers rise dramatically in the elderly.
source: Cancer is often associated with aging as the incidences of most cancers rise dramatically in the elderly (Bray et al., 2018; Aunan et al., 2017).
evidence: This epidemiological observation is supported by citations.

claim: Oncogene activation mediates tumor cells to adopt a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP).
source: Oncogene activation mediates tumor cells to adopt a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which fosters chronic inflammatory milieus (Faget et al., 2019; Fane and Weeraratna, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: SASP fosters chronic inflammatory milieus.
source: Oncogene activation mediates tumor cells to adopt a senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP), which fosters chronic inflammatory milieus (Faget et al., 2019; Fane and Weeraratna, 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The aging microenvironment induces senescence of T cells, which leads to immunosuppression in multiple types of malignancies.
source: Consequently, the aging microenvironment induces senescence of T cells, which leads to immunosuppression in multiple types of malignancies (Ye et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The tumor microenvironment (TME) can induce senescence of adoptively transferred tumor-specific T cells.
source: Furthermore, the tumor microenvironment (TME) can induce senescence of adoptively transferred tumor-specific T cells, and therefore develop a resistance to immunotherapy (Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: TME-induced senescence of T cells develops resistance to immunotherapy.
source: Furthermore, the tumor microenvironment (TME) can induce senescence of adoptively transferred tumor-specific T cells, and therefore develop a resistance to immunotherapy (Ye et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: EO771 LM-phenotype cells showed intense bioluminescence imaging (BLI) signals throughout tumors in the meningeal space after intracarotid artery injection.
source: Intense bioluminescence imaging (BLI) signals (Figure 1B and C) and hyperintense T1-weighted signals (Figure 1D) throughout tumors in the meningeal space demonstrated abundant neuro-anatomic metastases of mice injected with LM-phenotype cells, rather than the parental cells.
evidence: This is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: EO771 LM-phenotype cells showed hyperintense T1-weighted signals throughout tumors in the meningeal space after intracarotid artery injection.
source: Intense bioluminescence imaging (BLI) signals (Figure 1B and C) and hyperintense T1-weighted signals (Figure 1D) throughout tumors in the meningeal space demonstrated abundant neuro-anatomic metastases of mice injected with LM-phenotype cells, rather than the parental cells.
evidence: This is supported by MRI data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LM cell injection into the intracarotid artery significantly shortened animal survival compared to the parental cell.
source: Furthermore, LM cell injection into the intracarotid artery significantly shortened animal survival compared to the parental cell (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The gene expression profiles of EO771 parental, inter and LM-phenotype cells segregate independently.
source: Furthermore, principal component analysis (PCA) of the transcriptome confirmed that the gene expression profiles of EO771 parental, inter and LM-phenotype cells segregate independently (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There was a heterogeneity between LM population and its matched parental population.
source: Thus, there was a heterogeneity between LM population and its matched parental population.
evidence: This is inferred from the PCA data showing segregation of gene expression profiles.

claim: CD45+ immune cells increased in mice injected with parental or LM cells, compared with those injected with PBS.
source: We found that CD45+ immune cells increased in mice injected with parental or LM cells, compared with those injected with PBS, indicating that the meninges were inflamed after tumor inoculation.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The meninges were inflamed after tumor inoculation.
source: We found that CD45+ immune cells increased in mice injected with parental or LM cells, compared with those injected with PBS, indicating that the meninges were inflamed after tumor inoculation.
evidence: This is inferred from the increase in CD45+ immune cells.

claim: Meningeal immune cell numbers in the presence of LM dropped significantly in comparison with those injected with parental cells.
source: However, meningeal immune cell numbers in the presence of LM dropped significantly in comparison with those injected with parental cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only T cells were markedly decreased in LM among meninge-infiltrating immune cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that only T cells were markedly decreased in LM (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Accelerated intracranial tumor progression was observed in Rag2-/- mice compared with wild type C57BL/6 mice when LM-phenotype cells were injected via intracarotid arteries.
source: Compared with wild type (WT) C57BL/6 mice, accelerated intracranial tumor progression was observed in the Rag2-/- mice when LM-phenotype cells were injected via intracarotid arteries, which was evaluated by bioluminescent signals (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Tumor formation was significantly enhanced in nude mice compared to immunocompetent BALB/c mice when injected with 4T1 LM-phenotype cells.
source: Similarly, we injected 4T1 LM-phenotype cells into the immunodeficient nude mice and immunocompetent BALB/c mice, and observed that tumor formation was significantly enhanced in nude mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: Intracranial tumor growth dramatically increased in mice with CD8+ T cell depletion compared with IgG neutralization.
source: Analyzing the LM lesions by histopathology, we found that intracranial tumor growth dramatically increased in the mice with CD8+ T cell depletion compared with IgG neutralization (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Depletion of CD4+ T cells exhibited slight tumor regression, although the difference did not reach statistical significance.
source: By contrast, depletion of CD4+ T cells even exhibited slight tumor regression, although the difference did not reach statistical significance (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: CD8+ T cells play an important role in constraining intracranial tumor growth.
source: These results suggested that CD8+ T cells play an important role in constraining intracranial tumor growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the CD8+ T cell depletion experiments showing increased tumor growth.

claim: Evans blue injected into the cisterna magna can be detected in dCLNs after 30 min.
source: Therefore, to visualize CNS lymphatic drainage, we injected Evans blue into the cisterna magna and detected the presence of dye in dCLNs 30 min later (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by the Evans blue detection experiment shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Intracranial tumors arising in Rag2-/- mice were much smaller when receiving transferred CD8+ T cells, but not CD4+ T cells.
source: Interestingly, intracranial tumors arising in Rag2-/- mice was much smaller when receiving transferred CD8+ T cells, but not CD4+ T cells (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Mice receiving CD8+ T cells had longer overall survival than those receiving CD4+ T cells or PBS.
source: More importantly, mice receiving CD8+ T cells had longer overall survival than those receiving CD4+ T cells or PBS (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by survival data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: CD8+ T cells are crucial effectors in controlling LM.
source: These data suggested that CD8+ T cells are crucial effectors in controlling LM.
evidence: This is inferred from the adoptive transfer experiments showing CD8+ T cells reduce tumor burden and extend survival.

claim: OVA peptide/MHC class I complex, SIINFEKL/H2-Kb, was only detected on CD11c+ DCs in dCLNs but not in inguinal LNs and spleen after EO771-OVA injection.
source: Interestingly, OVA peptide/MHC class I complex, SIINFEKL/H2-Kb, was only detected on CD11c+ DCs in dCLNs but not the ones in inguinal LNs and spleen (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A significant proportion of OVA/SIINFEKL pentamer+ CD8+ T cells was detected in the dCLNs of mice injected with EO771-OVA cells, but not in mice injected with PBS, wild type EO771 or EO771-gB cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed that a significant proportion of OVA/SIINFEKL pentamer+ CD8+ T cells was detected in the dCLNs of mice injected with EO771-OVA cells, but not in the mice injected with PBS, wild type EO771 (EO771 WT) and EO771 with an irrelevant antigen glycoprotein B (EO771-gB) cells (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Only DCs from mice receiving EO771-OVA inoculation could expand OT-1 T cells.
source: Analysis of OT-1 T cell priming revealed that only DCs from mice receiving EO771-OVA inoculation could expand OT-1 T cells (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and induce a significant increase in IFN-γ production (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) of OT-1 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: DCs from mice receiving EO771-OVA inoculation induced a significant increase in IFN-γ production of OT-1 T cells.
source: Analysis of OT-1 T cell priming revealed that only DCs from mice receiving EO771-OVA inoculation could expand OT-1 T cells (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and induce a significant increase in IFN-γ production (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E) of OT-1 T cells.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Antigen processing was impaired in mice receiving surgical ligation of lymphatic afferent to dCLNs.
source: Determined by the expression of SIINFEKL/H2-Kb complex on the surface of CD11c+ dCLN DCs, antigen processing was impaired in the mice receiving surgical ligation (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The proliferation of OT-1 T cells primed by dCLN DCs was diminished after surgical ligation of lymphatic afferent to dCLNs.
source: In addition, the proliferation (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) and IFN-γ production (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) of OT-1 T cells primed by dCLN DCs were diminished.
evidence: This is supported by CFSE dilution data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: IFN-γ production of OT-1 T cells primed by dCLN DCs was diminished after surgical ligation of lymphatic afferent to dCLNs.
source: In addition, the proliferation (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) and IFN-γ production (Figure 3I, Figure 3—figure supplement 1H) of OT-1 T cells primed by dCLN DCs were diminished.
evidence: This is supported by ELISpot data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: dCLNs could generate tumor-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: Collectively, dCLNs could generate tumor-specific CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the experiments showing antigen presentation and T cell priming in dCLNs.

claim: The percentages of DTCs were not significantly different between mice injected with parental or LM cells.
source: We found that the percentages of DTCs were not significantly different between these two groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: CD8+ T cell transfusion did not influence the percentages of DTCs in the peripheral blood.
source: We found that CD8+ T cell transfusion did not influence the percentages of DTCs in the peripheral blood (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by DTC quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CD8+ T cells did not affect the dissemination of cancer cells.
source: These data suggested that CD8+ T cells did not affect the dissemination of cancer cells, probably the metastatic lesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the DTC analysis showing no difference with CD8+ T cell presence.

claim: The number of CD8+ T cells in meninges of mice injected with EO771 LM-phenotype cells was much lower than in mice injected with parental cells.
source: Then we observed that in the meninge, the number of CD8+ T cells of mice injected with EO771 LM-phenotype cells (LM-CD8+ T cells) was much lower than the one in mice injected with parental cells (Parental-CD8+ T cells) (Figure 4A and B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The absolute count of LM-CD8+ T cells in dCLNs was significantly lower than Parental-CD8+ T cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that the absolute count of LM-CD8+ T cells in dCLNs was significantly lower than Parental-CD8+ T cells (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: The proliferation of LM-CD8+ T cells in dCLNs was significantly decreased, compared with the dCLN Parental-CD8+ T cells.
source: Moreover, the proliferation of LM-CD8+ T cells in dCLNs was significantly decreased, compared with the dCLN Parental-CD8+ T cells, determined by flow cytometric analysis of CD8 and Ki-67 co-staining (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is supported by Ki-67 staining data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The decreased proliferation of CD8+ T cells in dCLNs was one of the reasons of low infiltration of CD8+ T cells in LM lesion.
source: These data suggested that the decreased proliferation of CD8+ T cells in dCLNs was one of the reasons of low infiltration of CD8+ T cells in LM lesion.
evidence: This is inferred from the proliferation data showing reduced Ki-67+ cells in LM-CD8+ T cells.

claim: LM- and Parental-CD8+ T cells have equivalent amount of cleaved caspase 3.
source: Determined by the apoptotic marker, cleaved caspase 3 expression, by flow cytometric analysis, LM- and Parental-CD8+ T cells have equivalent amount of cleaved caspase 3 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), indicating that apoptosis is not the major cause contributing to the impaired proliferation of T cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Apoptosis is not the major cause contributing to the impaired proliferation of T cells in LM.
source: Determined by the apoptotic marker, cleaved caspase 3 expression, by flow cytometric analysis, LM- and Parental-CD8+ T cells have equivalent amount of cleaved caspase 3 (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), indicating that apoptosis is not the major cause contributing to the impaired proliferation of T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the equivalent cleaved caspase 3 levels between LM and Parental CD8+ T cells.

claim: dCLN LM-CD8+ T cells showed distinctly increased expression of senescence markers p53 and p21 compared with dCLN Parental-CD8+ T cells.
source: We detected the distinct increased expression of senescence markers p53 and p21 in dCLN LM- CD8+ T cells compared with dCLN Parental-CD8+ T cells (Figure 4G, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: The percentage of senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal)-positive T cells was higher in the LM-CD8+ T cells.
source: Moreover, the percentage of senescence-associated β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal)-positive T cells was higher in the LM-CD8+ T cells (Figure 4H and I).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: CD8+ T cells in dCLNs of mice bearing LM exhibit senescence.
source: Collectively, CD8+ T cells in dCLNs of mice bearing LM exhibit senescence.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased expression of senescence markers (p53, p21, SA-β-gal) in LM-CD8+ T cells.

claim: The migration of LM-CD8+ T cells to meninges in vivo was significantly less than Parental-CD8+ T cells.
source: Two-photon live imaging showed that the migration of LM- CD8+ T cells to meninges in vivo was significantly less than Parental-CD8+ T cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that CD8+ T cells displayed impaired trafficking ability to meninges under LM.
evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CD8+ T cells displayed impaired trafficking ability to meninges under LM.
source: Two-photon live imaging showed that the migration of LM- CD8+ T cells to meninges in vivo was significantly less than Parental-CD8+ T cells (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that CD8+ T cells displayed impaired trafficking ability to meninges under LM.
evidence: This is inferred from the two-photon imaging showing reduced migration of LM-CD8+ T cells.

claim: VLA-4 levels in CD8+ T cells from both leptomeningeal space and dCLNs were downregulated in mice injected with LM-phenotype cells, compared with those of mice injected with parental cells.
source: We observed that VLA-4 levels in CD8+ T cells from both leptomeningeal space and those from dCLNs were downregulated in mice injected with LM-phenotype cells, compared with those of mice injected with parental cells (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VLA-4 blockade decreased the number of CD8+ T cell in meninges.
source: To evaluate the function of VLA-4 in breast cancer LM, we applied neutralization antibody against VLA-4 and found that VLA-4 blockade decreased the number of CD8+ T cell in meninges (Figure 5C), and aggregated intracranial tumor metastasis, determined by histopathology (Figure 5D) and BLI signaling (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: VLA-4 blockade aggregated intracranial tumor metastasis.
source: To evaluate the function of VLA-4 in breast cancer LM, we applied neutralization antibody against VLA-4 and found that VLA-4 blockade decreased the number of CD8+ T cell in meninges (Figure 5C), and aggregated intracranial tumor metastasis, determined by histopathology (Figure 5D) and BLI signaling (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This is supported by histopathology and BLI data shown in Figure 5D, E, and F.

claim: Parental-CD8+ T cells with higher expression of VLA-4 exhibited specific adhesion to plate-bound VCAM-1 protein (74.77 ± 4.27%).
source: Parental-CD8+ T cells with higher expression of VLA-4 exhibited specific adhesion to plate-bound VCAM-1 protein (74.77 ± 4.27%), whereas LM- CD8+ T cells with lower expression of VLA-4 displayed only background levels of adhesion (9.96 ± 0.89%).
evidence: This is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: LM-CD8+ T cells with lower expression of VLA-4 displayed only background levels of adhesion to VCAM-1 (9.96 ± 0.89%).
source: Parental-CD8+ T cells with higher expression of VLA-4 exhibited specific adhesion to plate-bound VCAM-1 protein (74.77 ± 4.27%), whereas LM- CD8+ T cells with lower expression of VLA-4 displayed only background levels of adhesion (9.96 ± 0.89%).
evidence: This is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Pretreatment of Parental-CD8+ T cells with the anti-VLA-4 neutralizing antibody virtually ablated their ability to adhere to VCAM-1 (19.22 ± 3.44%).
source: Pretreatment of Parental-CD8+ T cells with the anti-VLA-4 neutralizing antibody virtually ablated their ability to adhere to VCAM-1 (19.22 ± 3.44%), while LM-CD8+ T cells pretreated with the anti-VLA-4 antibody showed no difference in their ability to adhere to VCAM-1 (8.43 ± 0.85%) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: LM-CD8+ T cells pretreated with the anti-VLA-4 antibody showed no difference in their ability to adhere to VCAM-1 (8.43 ± 0.85%).
source: Pretreatment of Parental-CD8+ T cells with the anti-VLA-4 neutralizing antibody virtually ablated their ability to adhere to VCAM-1 (19.22 ± 3.44%), while LM-CD8+ T cells pretreated with the anti-VLA-4 antibody showed no difference in their ability to adhere to VCAM-1 (8.43 ± 0.85%) (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by adhesion assay data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The migration of Parental-CD8+ T cells was much stronger than LM-CD8+ T cells in an in vitro BBB model.
source: We observed that the migration of Parental-CD8+ T cells was much stronger than LM-CD8+ T cells, which was disrupted by anti-VLA4 treatment (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Migration of Parental-CD8+ T cells was disrupted by anti-VLA4 treatment.
source: We observed that the migration of Parental-CD8+ T cells was much stronger than LM-CD8+ T cells, which was disrupted by anti-VLA4 treatment (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: VLA-4 blockade had no effect on the proliferation of dCLN CD8+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, VLA-4 blockade had no effect on the proliferation (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and cell death (Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) of dCLN CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by Ki-67 staining data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: VLA-4 blockade had no effect on cell death of dCLN CD8+ T cells.
source: Furthermore, VLA-4 blockade had no effect on the proliferation (Figure 5I, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D) and cell death (Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E) of dCLN CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by cleaved caspase-3 staining data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Blocking VLA-4 in CD8+ T cells inhibited their adhesion and migration, leading to the impaired recruitment to meninges and lack of the capacity to control LM.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that blocking VLA-4 in CD8+ T cells inhibited their adhesion and migration, leading to the impaired recruitment to meninges and lack of the capacity to control LM.
evidence: This is inferred from the VLA-4 blockade experiments showing reduced adhesion, migration, and increased tumor burden.

claim: p53 was predicted to bind to VLA-4 promoter by three different algorithms (JASPAR, PROMO, and TFBIND).
source: To further explore the mechanisms for VLA-4 downregulation in LM-CD8+ T cells, we predicted the possible transcription factors binding to VLA-4 promoter by three different algorithms (JASPAR, PROMO, and TFBIND). Interestingly, we found p53, the senescence marker, which functions as a transcription factor involved in a myriad of cellular activities (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction using bioinformatics algorithms.

claim: p53 knockout restored VLA-4 levels of CD8+ T cells in Trp53-/- mice inoculated with LM-EO771 cells.
source: We found that VLA-4 levels in dCLN CD8+ T cells were lower in WT mice injected with LM-EO771 cells. By comparison, p53 knockout restored VLA-4 levels of CD8+ T cells in Trp53-/- mice inoculated with LM-EO771 cells (Figure 6A), suggesting that p53 mediated VLA-4 suppression in CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: p53 mediated VLA-4 suppression in CD8+ T cells.
source: We found that VLA-4 levels in dCLN CD8+ T cells were lower in WT mice injected with LM-EO771 cells. By comparison, p53 knockout restored VLA-4 levels of CD8+ T cells in Trp53-/- mice inoculated with LM-EO771 cells (Figure 6A), suggesting that p53 mediated VLA-4 suppression in CD8+ T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the restoration of VLA-4 levels in p53-deficient mice.

claim: One putative p53-binding site is located at –1550 to –1525 bp upstream of the VLA-4(Itga4) transcription start site (TSS).
source: In silico analyses performed with three different algorithms (JASPAR, PROMO, and TFBIND) predicted one putative p53-binding site located at –1550 to –1525 bp upstream of the VLA-4(Itga4) transcription start site (TSS) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on computational prediction shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Upon p53 forced expression, the luciferase signal of EL4 cells transfected with full-length Itga4 TSS decreased.
source: Upon p53 forced expression, the luciferase signal of EL4 cells transfected with full-length Itga4 TSS decreased.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Mutation of p53-binding site abolished the suppression of luciferase activity.
source: Moreover, mutation of p53-binding site abolished the suppression of luciferase activity (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: An average of 4.26-fold enrichment was obtained with anti-p53 antibody in the LM-CD8+ T cells in ChIP-qPCR.
source: To confirm these results in an endogenous setting, we performed chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP)–qPCR with an antibody against p53 and found an average of 4.26-fold enrichment was obtained with anti-p53 antibody in the LM-CD8+ T cells compared to ChIP with a control immunoglobulin G (IgG).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: An average of 1.03-fold enrichment was found in Parental-CD8+ T cells in ChIP-qPCR with anti-p53 antibody.
source: By contrast, an average of 1.03-fold enrichment was found in Parental-CD8+ T cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In Trp53-/- mice, the senescence of CD8+ T cells was prevented as a result of p53 deficiency.
source: In Trp53-/- mice, the senescence of CD8+ T cells was prevented as a result of p53 deficiency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), contributing to upregulation of VLA-4 (Figure 6A) and enhanced trafficking ability to meninges (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by SA-β-gal staining data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: p53 deficiency contributed to upregulation of VLA-4 and enhanced trafficking ability to meninges.
source: In Trp53-/- mice, the senescence of CD8+ T cells was prevented as a result of p53 deficiency (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), contributing to upregulation of VLA-4 (Figure 6A) and enhanced trafficking ability to meninges (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by VLA-4 expression and two-photon imaging data.

claim: Tumor growth was inhibited in P53-deficient mice.
source: Therefore, tumor growth was inhibited in P53-deficient mice determined by BLI signal (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This is supported by BLI data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E and F.

claim: VLA-4 transcription in T cells in LM is suppressed by the senescence factor p53.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrated that VLA-4 transcription in T cells in LM is suppressed by the senescence factor p53.
evidence: This is the conclusion drawn from the luciferase assays, ChIP-qPCR, and p53 knockout experiments.

claim: The proportion of SA-β-gal+CD8+ T cells was higher in CSF from metastatic patients compared with those of nonmalignant neurological disease patients.
source: We found that the proportion of SA-β-gal+CD8+ T cells was higher in CSF from metastatic patients compared with those of nonmalignant neurological disease patients (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), indicating that intracranial CD8+ T cells experienced senescence in patients with LM.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from patient samples shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Intracranial CD8+ T cells experienced senescence in patients with LM.
source: We found that the proportion of SA-β-gal+CD8+ T cells was higher in CSF from metastatic patients compared with those of nonmalignant neurological disease patients (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), indicating that intracranial CD8+ T cells experienced senescence in patients with LM.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased SA-β-gal+ CD8+ T cells in LM patients.

claim: CSF CD8+ T cells of metastatic patients had lower expression of VLA-4.
source: Moreover, flow cytometry analysis showed the CSF CD8+ T cells of metastatic patients had lower expression of VLA-4 (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data from patient samples shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The percentage of SA-β-gal+CD8+ T cells was negatively correlated with VLA-4 levels in CD8+ T cells of LM patients.
source: Moreover, the percentage of SA-β-gal+CD8+ T cells was negatively correlated with VLA-4 levels in CD8+ T cells of LM patients (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The brain has been considered as an immune-privileged organ due to the blood-brain barrier limiting access of circulating immune cells.
source: Access of circulating immune cells to the brain is limited by the blood–brain barrier (BBB). Therefore, the brain has previously been considered as an immune-privileged organ.
evidence: This is a logical inference connecting BBB function to the concept of immune privilege.

claim: The identification of functional lymphatic vessels in meninges has shifted the paradigm of brain immune privilege.
source: Recently, the paradigm has shifted, as functional lymphatic vessels have been identified in meninges.
evidence: This implies that the discovery of meningeal lymphatics changed the understanding of brain immunity.

claim: Senescent cells are characterized by withdrawal from the cell cycle and loss of the capability to proliferate under stimuli of growth factors or mitogens.
source: On the other hand, senescent cells exhibit stress signs, which is characterized by withdrawal from the cell cycle and loss of the capability to proliferate under stimuli of growth factors or mitogens (Montes et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cellular senescence supported by a citation.

claim: The VLA-4-VCAM-1 pathway plays an important role in T cell leptomeningeal recruitment.
source: The very late activated Ag-4 (VLA-4)-vascular adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) pathway plays an important role in T cell leptomeningeal recruitment (Theien et al., 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Evans blue is widely used as a marker of the BBB integrity.
source: Evans blue, which is widely used as a marker of the BBB integrity, can be preferentially drained via the lymphatics (Maloveska et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Evans blue usage supported by a citation.

claim: Evans blue can be preferentially drained via the lymphatics.
source: Evans blue, which is widely used as a marker of the BBB integrity, can be preferentially drained via the lymphatics (Maloveska et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation.

claim: The priming of tumor-specific CD8+ T cells primarily relies on antigen-presenting DCs.
source: The priming of tumor-specific CD8+ T cells primarily relies on antigen-presenting DCs, which is the fundamental step that launches T cell response against tumor (Bandola-Simon and Roche, 2019; Alfei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DC-mediated priming is the fundamental step that launches T cell response against tumor.
source: The priming of tumor-specific CD8+ T cells primarily relies on antigen-presenting DCs, which is the fundamental step that launches T cell response against tumor (Bandola-Simon and Roche, 2019; Alfei et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Meningeal lymphatics act as an avenue for CNS drainage and immune cell trafficking.
source: Meningeal lymphatics act as an avenue for CNS drainage and immune cell trafficking (Tavares and Louveau, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Adaptive immune response against tumor was provoked by antigen-specific CD8+ T cells.
source: Adaptive immune response against tumor was provoked by antigen-specific CD8+ T cells (Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established immunological knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Tumor-specific CD8+ T cells are primed by DCs in dCLNs, migrate to meninges, and recognize and lyse tumor cells.
source: It is well known that tumor-specific CD8+ T cells were primed by DCs in dCLNs, migrated to meninges, and recognized and lysed tumor cells (Calzascia et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about T cell function supported by a citation.

claim: Increased senescent T cells resulted in T cell proliferation arrest and killing capacity defect.
source: Previous studies have indicated that increased senescent T cells resulted in T cell proliferation arrest and killing capacity defect (Ye and Peng, 2015; Appay et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: VLA-4 is responsible for CNS tropism of T cells.
source: VLA-4 is responsible for CNS tropism of T cells and VLA-4 neutralization can inhibit the homing and infiltration of antigen-specific T cells in cerebral autoimmune models (Burkly et al., 1994; Zundler et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: VLA-4 neutralization can inhibit the homing and infiltration of antigen-specific T cells in cerebral autoimmune models.
source: VLA-4 is responsible for CNS tropism of T cells and VLA-4 neutralization can inhibit the homing and infiltration of antigen-specific T cells in cerebral autoimmune models (Burkly et al., 1994; Zundler et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Induction of p53 plays a direct role in cellular senescence.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that induction of p53 plays a direct role in cellular senescence.
evidence: This is established knowledge about p53 function in senescence.

claim: p53 activation primarily responds to the DNA damage response (DDR) caused by telomere attrition, oxidative, or oncogenic stress.
source: Its activation primarily responds to the DNA damage response (DDR) caused by telomere attrition, oxidative, or oncogenic stress (Mijit et al., 2020; Kumari and Jat, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Several p53 targets and regulators have been associated with induction of senescence.
source: Also, several p53 targets and regulators have been associated with induction of senescence (Feng et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: p53-deficient T cells exhibited decreased apoptosis.
source: In addition, in line with our study, previous studies showed that p53-deficient T cells exhibited decreased apoptosis (Madapura et al., 2012) and enhanced proliferation in T cells (Banerjee et al., 2016), supporting that p53-deficient T cells have higher anti-tumor effector function.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: p53-deficient T cells exhibited enhanced proliferation.
source: In addition, in line with our study, previous studies showed that p53-deficient T cells exhibited decreased apoptosis (Madapura et al., 2012) and enhanced proliferation in T cells (Banerjee et al., 2016), supporting that p53-deficient T cells have higher anti-tumor effector function.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: p53-deficient T cells have higher anti-tumor effector function.
source: In addition, in line with our study, previous studies showed that p53-deficient T cells exhibited decreased apoptosis (Madapura et al., 2012) and enhanced proliferation in T cells (Banerjee et al., 2016), supporting that p53-deficient T cells have higher anti-tumor effector function.
evidence: This is inferred from the decreased apoptosis and enhanced proliferation of p53-deficient T cells.

claim: Tumor-specific immunity originated from draining dCLNs is essential for restraining LM.
source: Collectively, our findings revealed that tumor-specific immunity originated from draining dCLNs is essential for restraining LM.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Senescence signals inhibit trafficking of CD8+ T cells from dCLNs to meninges and therefore promote the progression of LM.
source: Senescence signals inhibit trafficking of CD8+ T cells from dCLNs to meninges and therefore promote the progression of LM.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing senescence impairs T cell trafficking.

claim: Rag2-/- mice lack mature T or B cells.
source: To confirm the role of T lymphocytes in LM, we injected EO771 LM-phenotype cells into Rag2-/- mice, which carry a targeted knockout mutation in recombination activating gene 2 (Rag2) and therefore lack mature T or B cells (Fan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Rag2-/- mice supported by a citation.

claim: Most of the immune surveillance takes place in the tumor draining lymph nodes (TDLN) largely as a result of its unique cellular composition and proximity to the primary tumor.
source: Most of the immune surveillance takes place in the tumor draining lymph nodes (TDLN) largely as a result of its unique cellular composition and proximity to the primary tumor (Chandrasekaran and King, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: dCLNs communicate with meningeal lymphatics directly.
source: It has been reported that dCLNs communicate with meningeal lymphatics directly (Louveau et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In brain tumors such as glioblastoma and brain metastases, the infiltrating T cells are dysfunctioned due to tolerance and exhaustion induced by the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment.
source: In brain tumors such as glioblastoma and brain metastases, the infiltrating T cells are dysfunctioned due to tolerance and exhaustion induced by the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (Farber et al., 2016; Woroniecka et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Immunosenescence is an important state of T cell dysfunction and responsible for immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment.
source: Emerging evidence suggests that immunosenescence, which is distinct from exhaustion, is an important state of T cell dysfunction and responsible for immunosuppression in the tumor microenvironment (Nikolich-Žugich, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: T cells undergo senescence in the normal aging process or in patients with chronic infections and cancers.
source: In recent studies, T cells undergo senescence in the normal aging process or in the patients with under chronic infections and cancers (Zhao et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: T cell senescence has been found to be strongly induced in several types of malignancies, including lung cancer, ovarian cancer, and melanoma through MAPK signaling.
source: T cell senescence has also been found to be strongly induced in several types of malignancies, including lung cancer (Chen et al., 2014), ovarian cancer (Wu et al., 2017), and melanoma (López-Otín et al., 2013) through MAPK signaling (Wang et al., 2002).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: MAPK/p38 signaling is essential for activating the cell cycle regulatory molecules p53, p21, and p16.
source: MAPK/p38 signaling is essential for activating the cell cycle regulatory molecules p53, p21, and p16, which might inhibit cell cycle progression to slow or completely arrest DNA replication and induce cell senescence (Montes et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: p53, p21, and p16 might inhibit cell cycle progression to slow or completely arrest DNA replication and induce cell senescence.
source: MAPK/p38 signaling is essential for activating the cell cycle regulatory molecules p53, p21, and p16, which might inhibit cell cycle progression to slow or completely arrest DNA replication and induce cell senescence (Montes et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior work.
